1.word_for_word: caturviṃśe — in the twenty-fourth chapter; mahendrasya makham vyāvartya hetubhiḥ — turning aside Mahendra's sacrifice by arguments; govardhana-makha-utsavam pravartayāmāsa — Kṛṣṇa instituted the Govardhana festival; bhūsurāṇām kriyā-garvam nirasya — having removed the ritual pride of the earthly gods, the brāhmaṇas; svaḥ-sureṣu ca — and among the gods of heaven; maghavan-mada-bhaṅgāya — to break Indra's pride; tan-makham samavārayat — he stopped that sacrifice; brāhmaṇāḥ kaṃsāt bhītāḥ — the brāhmaṇas, afraid of Kaṃsa; svāśrama-sthāḥ eva bhagavantam abhajan — worshiped Bhagavān while remaining in their own āśramas; indra-yāge kṛta-udyamān gopān apaśyat — he saw the cowherds making preparations for Indra's sacrifice
1.translation: In the twenty-fourth chapter, Kṛṣṇa used various arguments to turn aside the sacrifice to Mahendra and instituted the Govardhana festival. Having already removed the pride in ritual action from the earthly gods, the brāhmaṇas, he now acted among the heavenly gods: in order to break Indra's pride he stopped Indra's sacrifice. The brāhmaṇas, afraid of Kaṃsa, worshiped Bhagavān while remaining in their own āśramas. Bhagavān, who was living there in Vraja, saw the cowherds making energetic preparations for the Indra sacrifice.

3.word_for_word: vṛthā sambhramaḥ na bhavati — this bustle cannot be purposeless; makhaḥ ayam iti evaṃ cet — if this is indeed a sacrifice; kim atra phalam — what is its result; kā devatā — who is the deity; kena adhikāriṇā — by what qualified performer; kena vā sādhanena sādhyate — by what means is it accomplished
3.translation: ‘Surely all this bustle is not pointless. If this is a sacrifice, then what is its fruit? Who is its deity? Who is qualified to perform it, and by what means is it accomplished?’

4-5.word_for_word: etat brūhi — tell me this; mahān kāmaḥ mama śravaṇe vartate — I have a great desire to hear; yad vā tava mahān kāmaḥ dṛśyate — or: a great eagerness is visible in you; tūṣṇīm sthitam prati āha — he speaks again to Nanda when he remains silent; sarvātmanām — of those who see the Self everywhere; sarvatra ātma-dṛṣṭīnām — whose vision sees the Self in all; na vidyate svaḥ paraḥ iti dṛṣṭiḥ — there is no vision of ‘own’ and ‘other’; amitra-ādayaḥ api na santi — therefore categories such as enemy do not truly exist for them; na mitram udāste udāsīnaḥ vidviṭ vā — no friend, neutral person or hater is excluded; teṣām kṛtyam sarvam na gopanīyam — none of their actions need be concealed; saty api bheda-darśane — even when practical distinctions are perceived; udāsīnaḥ śatruvat varjyaḥ — a merely indifferent person may be excluded like an enemy; suhṛt-mantreṣu na varjanīyaḥ — but a true well-wisher is not to be excluded from counsel
4-5.translation: ‘Tell me about it; I have a great desire to hear.’ Alternatively, the sense may be, ‘I can see that you yourself are greatly intent upon this.’ When Nanda remains silent, Kṛṣṇa continues: those who see the Self in all beings do not ultimately maintain the distinction ‘mine’ and ‘other.’ Therefore fixed categories such as enemy, friend or neutral do not exist for them, and there is no action that must be hidden from a genuine well-wisher. Even where practical distinctions remain, an indifferent person may be left out of confidential deliberation just as an enemy is, but a true friend, being like oneself, should not be excluded.

6.word_for_word: suhṛdbhiḥ saha vicārya — after deliberating with friends; jñātvā eva karma kartavyam — action should be performed only after understanding it; na tu gata-anugatikatva-mātreṇa — not merely by blindly following precedent; ajñātvā ca — if performed without understanding; viduṣaḥ yathā tat-karma-phalam syāt — the same action bears its fruit for one who knows; tathā na aviduṣaḥ — but not in the same way for one who does not know
6.translation: An action should be undertaken after discussion with trusted friends and after understanding it, not merely by following what others have done. The fruit of an act performed with understanding does not accrue in the same way to one who performs it without understanding.

7.word_for_word: bhavatām ayam kriyā-yogaḥ — this ritual undertaking of yours; śāstrataḥ api kim vicāritaḥ pravṛttaḥ — was it begun after scriptural consideration; laukika-ācāra-prāptaḥ vā — or has it merely come down through customary practice; sādhu sa-upapattikam bhaṇyatām — explain it properly together with its reasoning
7.translation: ‘Was this ritual undertaking begun after examination of scripture, or has it simply come down to you as local custom? Explain it to me clearly, together with the reasons for it.’

8.word_for_word: parjanyaḥ — Parjanya, the rain-god; vṛṣṭi-dvārā bhagavān īśvaraḥ — as lord through the agency of rain; prīṇanam santarpakam jīvanam — life-giving water that nourishes and satisfies; mṛta-prāyāṇām tṛṇa-ādīnām prāṇadam — giving life to grasses and other vegetation that are nearly dead
8.translation: Parjanya is regarded as lord because, through rain, he supplies the nourishing water of life, restoring vitality to grasses and other plants that have become almost dead.

9.word_for_word: tataḥ kim iti — ‘what follows from that?’; vayam ca anye narāḥ — we and other people; vār-mucām patim īśvaram — the lord of the rain-bearing clouds; tad-retasā siddhaiḥ dravyaiḥ — with materials produced through his rain; kratubhiḥ yajanti — worship him through sacrifices
9.translation: ‘And what follows from this?’ We, and other people as well, worship the lord of the rain-clouds with sacrifices whose materials have themselves been produced through his rain.

10.word_for_word: upajīvanti upajīvikām kalpayanti — they obtain and maintain their livelihood; dharma-artha-kāma-siddhaye — for the attainment of dharma, wealth and desire; nanu kṛṣi-ādibhiḥ jīvanti kim indreṇa — objection: people live by agriculture and the like, so what need is there of Indra; puṃsām phala-bhāvanaḥ — he is the producer of people's results; parjanyam vinā kṛṣi-ādi-vaiphalyāt — because agriculture and similar activities fail without rain
10.translation: People secure their livelihood in this way for the attainment of dharma, wealth and enjoyment. One may ask, ‘Do they not live by farming and similar work? What need have they of Indra?’ The answer is that Indra is the producer of the result, because farming and the rest fail without rain.

12.word_for_word: indrāya manyum janayan — deliberately arousing Indra's anger; kopa-janana-dvārā — by creating that anger; garva-parvatāt indram avatārayitum — in order to bring Indra down from the mountain of pride; devatā-nirākaraṇam — the apparent rejection of the deity; na tu ayam eva abhiprāyaḥ — this is not Kṛṣṇa's final doctrinal intention
12.translation: Kṛṣṇa's apparent rejection of the deity is intended to provoke Indra's anger and thereby bring him down from the mountain of pride. Śrīdhara expressly notes that this polemical argument is not Kṛṣṇa's ultimate doctrinal position.

13.word_for_word: prathamam tāvat karma-vādena devān nirākaroti — first he dismisses the gods by adopting the doctrine of ritual action; jaḍāt karmaṇaḥ kevalāt katham phala-siddhiḥ — objection: how can inert action by itself produce a result; aśīlita-mīmāṃsānām — of those untrained in Mīmāṃsā; ati-vilasitā śraddhā — such an objection displays excessive confidence; karmaṇām phala-kāraṇatve vacanataḥ avagate — when scripture itself establishes ritual acts as causes of results; kim tataḥ anupapannam — what impossibility remains
13.translation: First Kṛṣṇa rejects dependence upon the gods by speaking from the standpoint of ritualism. If one objects, ‘How can an inert act by itself produce a result?’ Śrīdhara replies in the voice of that position: such doubt belongs to one insufficiently trained in Mīmāṃsā; once scriptural injunction establishes ritual action as a cause of its result, what impossibility remains?

14.word_for_word: kecit ati-sāhasa-bhītāḥ — some, afraid of so extreme a claim; karma-paratantram īśvaram manyante — regard Īśvara as dependent upon karma; tat-matam anūdya nirākaroti — he states that view and then rejects it; svayam karmabhiḥ aliptaḥ — though himself untouched by karma; anyeṣām jīvānām karmaṇām phala-rūpī phala-dātā — as giver of the fruits of other beings' actions; kartāram bhajate — he attends to the agent; tat-tat-karma-phala-dānena — by awarding each corresponding result
14.translation: Some, shrinking from the extreme claim that ritual acts operate entirely by themselves, suppose that Īśvara exists but is bound to administer karma. Kṛṣṇa next states and rejects that position: although Īśvara himself is untouched by karma, on this view he merely serves the doer by handing out the corresponding result of each action.

15.word_for_word: karmaṇaḥ eva phala-siddheḥ — because the result is said to arise from karma itself; tat-pāratantrye — and if Īśvara is dependent upon it; ajā-gala-stana-tulyatvāt — he becomes as useless as the teats on a goat's neck; na devatayā kṛtyam — there is therefore no need of a deity; nanu karmaṇaḥ api pravṛttiḥ antaryāmi-apekṣā — objection: even the arising of action depends on the inner controller; svabhāva-vihitam karma — action prescribed by one's own nature; svabhāvena prāktana-saṃskāreṇa — by nature, that is, previous impressions; anyathā kartum anīśena — by one powerless to act otherwise
15.translation: If the result is produced by karma itself and even Īśvara is subordinated to it, then a deity would be functionless, like the useless teats on a goat's neck. One may object that even action depends upon the inner controller. Kṛṣṇa answers, still within his polemical argument, that action is prescribed by one's own nature—that is, by impressions from previous acts—and the individual is powerless to act otherwise.

16.word_for_word: svabhāva-tantraḥ — governed by one's nature; pravṛtteḥ saṃskāra-adhīnatvāt — because activity depends upon latent impressions; kim antaryāmiṇā — what need, on this argument, is there of an inner controller
16.translation: He elaborates: the living being is governed by its own nature. Since its activity follows prior impressions, the polemical conclusion is, ‘What need is there to posit an inner controller?’

17.word_for_word: svabhāvataḥ niṣpannasya karmaṇaḥ eva sarva-kāraṇatvāt — because action arising from one's nature is being treated as the cause of everything; karma eva pūjyam — action itself should therefore be worshiped; dehān iti sārdhena — this is stated in the verse and a half beginning with ‘bodies’
17.translation: Thus, from the standpoint that action arising from one's nature is the cause of all results, Kṛṣṇa reaches the provisional conclusion that action itself is what should be honored. This is expressed in the following verse and a half.

18.word_for_word: sampūjayet — one should honor; nanu devatā-uddeśena dravya-tyāga-ātmakatvāt karmaṇaḥ — objection: sacrifice consists of giving up materials for a deity; katham devatām vinā siddhiḥ — how can it be accomplished without the deity; karma-aṅga-mātram devatā iti pakṣam — treating the deity as merely an accessory of the ritual; hetu-vādam āśritya — adopting causal reasoning; anyām eva devatām samarthayate — he proceeds to establish a different object of worship; añjasā iti — with the verse beginning ‘directly’
18.translation: ‘One should worship’ means ‘one should honor.’ An objection arises: since sacrifice consists in relinquishing offerings for a deity, how can ritual succeed without a deity? Kṛṣṇa now seems to summarize the Mīmāṃsaka idea that the deity is merely an accessory to the act, but then, using causal reasoning, he turns toward establishing a different and more immediate object of worship, beginning with the verse ‘directly…’

19.word_for_word: hetu-balena eva vipakṣe doṣam āha — by the force of causal reasoning he points out the defect in the opposing position; ājīvya iti — by the word ‘source of livelihood’; upajīvati — one lives upon; sevate — one serves or depends upon
19.translation: By causal reasoning he points out the defect in worshiping what is not one's actual support. ‘Ājīvya’ means that upon which one lives and which one therefore serves or depends upon.

20.word_for_word: sva-vṛttim vaktum — in order to state their own occupation; dṛṣṭāntatvena varṇānām vṛtti-bhedam āha — he gives, as an example, the differing occupations of the social classes; brāhmaṇā vedādhyāpana-ādinā — a brāhmaṇa lives by teaching the Veda and related duties
20.translation: To identify the cowherds' own proper livelihood, Kṛṣṇa first illustrates how occupations differ according to social class: a brāhmaṇa, for example, lives by teaching the Veda and by the other duties proper to him.

21.word_for_word: vaiśya-vṛtteḥ cātur-vidhyam — the fourfold livelihood of a vaiśya; kṛṣi — agriculture; vāṇijya — trade; go-rakṣā — cow protection; etat trayam — these are three; kusīdam — lending at interest; vṛddhi-jīvanam — living from increase or interest; caturtham — the fourth
21.translation: The occupation of a vaiśya is fourfold: agriculture, trade and cow protection are the first three; the fourth is lending money at interest, living from its increase.

22.word_for_word: nanu gavām api vṛttiḥ mahendra-adhīnā eva — objection: even the livelihood of cattle depends upon Mahendra; nirīśvara-sāṅkhya-mata-āśrayeṇa nirākaroti — Kṛṣṇa rejects this by temporarily adopting nontheistic Sāṅkhya reasoning; sattvam iti śloka-dvayena — in the two verses beginning ‘sattva’; anyonyam strī-puruṣa-yogena — ‘with one another’ means through the union of female and male
22.translation: One may object that even the cattle's livelihood ultimately depends upon Mahendra's rain. Kṛṣṇa answers this, for the sake of his argument, by temporarily adopting the causal scheme of nontheistic Sāṅkhya in the next two verses. ‘With one another’ refers to the interaction or union of male and female and, more broadly, of natural causes.

23.word_for_word: sarvataḥ iti — ‘everywhere’; samudra-śila-uṣara-ādiṣu api vṛṣṭi-darśanāt — because rain is seen even over ocean, rocks and barren land; na prekṣāvat-pūrvakatvam vṛṣṭeḥ — rain therefore does not appear to be purposively directed by an intelligent agent; taiḥ eva meghaiḥ eva — by those very clouds themselves; sidhyanti jīvanti — creatures prosper and live
23.translation: The word ‘everywhere’ supports the argument: rain falls even upon the ocean, rocks and barren ground, so its distribution does not appear to proceed from deliberate discrimination by an intelligent agent. Living beings prosper through those clouds themselves.

24.word_for_word: tathāpi yoga-kṣema-artham devatā-apekṣā iti cet — objection: even so, a deity is needed for acquisition and preservation; na naḥ puraḥ iti — he answers with ‘we have no cities’; puraḥ — towns; janapadāḥ — settled countries; asmākam yoga-kṣema-hetuḥ — the cause of our livelihood and security; vana-śaila-ādayaḥ eva — forests, mountains and the like alone
24.translation: If one says that a deity is nevertheless needed for securing and preserving one's livelihood, Kṛṣṇa answers, ‘We have no cities or settled kingdoms.’ For cowherds, forests, mountains and the other features of their own environment are the immediate basis of livelihood and security.

25.word_for_word: brāhmaṇān api saṅgṛhṇan — including the brāhmaṇas as well; nigamayati — he brings the argument to its conclusion; tasmāt iti — with ‘therefore’; svayam utprekṣita-yāga-prayoga-kalpanām āha — he now proposes a sacrificial procedure of his own conception; ye indra-yāga-sambhārāḥ — the materials assembled for Indra's sacrifice; sambhārāḥ sādhanāni — ‘materials’ means the ritual requisites
25.translation: Kṛṣṇa concludes while including the brāhmaṇas in the new rite as well. Beginning with ‘therefore,’ he proposes a sacrificial procedure of his own design: the very materials that had been assembled for Indra's sacrifice are to be redirected. ‘Sambhāra’ means the collection of ritual requisites.

26.word_for_word: sūpam — pulse soup; maudgam — prepared from mung beans; pāyasam — food cooked purely in milk; saṃyāva-ādayaḥ — preparations such as saṃyāva; go-dhūma-ādi-vikriyāḥ — products made from wheat and the like; kramaḥ — the prescribed sequence; sūpa-pāyasayoḥ śrutyā — for soup and milk preparation, according to scripture; dohasya arthataḥ — for milking, by implication; anyeṣām pāṭhataḥ — for the others, from the textual order
26.translation: ‘Sūpa’ is a soup of pulses, here especially mung; ‘pāyasa’ is a preparation cooked in milk; and saṃyāva and the others are preparations made from wheat and similar grains. The sequence is established scripturally for the soup and pāyasa, by implication for the milking, and for the remaining items by the order in which they are mentioned.

27.word_for_word: yāga-śobhā-artham — for the splendor of the sacrifice; śraddhā-utpādana-artham ca — and to generate faith; hūyantām iti — he says ‘let offerings be made’; dhenu-dakṣiṇāḥ — fees consisting of cows, or fees accompanied by cows; vaḥ yuṣmābhiḥ — ‘by you’
27.translation: For the dignity of the sacrifice and also to inspire faith, Kṛṣṇa says, ‘Let offerings be made.’ ‘Cow-dakṣiṇās’ may mean gifts consisting of cows, or sacrificial fees accompanied by cows; ‘vaḥ’ means ‘by you.’

30.word_for_word: sarvān śiraḥ-kampena anumodayan — approving them all with a nod of the head; go-brāhmaṇa-adrīṇām iti — he speaks of the cows, brāhmaṇas and mountain; mahyam — to me; mama ca — and to myself
30.translation: Approving everyone's assent with a nod of his head, Kṛṣṇa speaks of worshiping the cows, the brāhmaṇas and the mountain. ‘Mahyam’ means ‘to me,’ that is, ‘to myself as well.’

32.word_for_word: tat-dravyeṇa — with those materials; tena mahendra-makha-dravyeṇa — with the very materials intended for Mahendra's sacrifice; girim dvijān prati — toward the mountain and the brāhmaṇas; yathā-yatham — each in the appropriate manner
32.translation: They used the very materials that had been prepared for Mahendra's sacrifice, offering them appropriately to Govardhana and to the brāhmaṇas.

33.word_for_word: balīn upahṛtya — having brought offerings; dattvā — having presented them; ādṛtāḥ — respectful; sādaraḥ — full of reverence
33.translation: They presented the various offerings with sincere respect and reverence.

34.word_for_word: anaḍud-yuktāni — yoked with bulls; uttama-anaḍudbhiḥ yuktāni — drawn by excellent bulls; sa-dvija-āśiṣaḥ — accompanied by the blessings of brāhmaṇas
34.translation: The carts were drawn by excellent bulls, and the people proceeded accompanied by the blessings of the brāhmaṇas.

35.word_for_word: gopa-viśrambhaṇam — producing confidence in the cowherds; gopānām viśvāsa-janakam rūpam gataḥ — assuming a form that generated their faith; balim upahāram ādat — he received the offering; abhakṣayat — he ate it
35.translation: To strengthen the cowherds' confidence, Kṛṣṇa assumed a form that visibly inspired their faith and, in that form as Govardhana, received and ate the offerings.

36.word_for_word: tasmai ātmane — to that manifestation who was himself; ātmanā svayam — by himself personally; vraja-janaiḥ saha — together with the people of Vraja; namaḥ-cakre — he bowed down; aho iti sārdha-ślokam paṭhan — reciting the verse and a half beginning ‘aho’
36.translation: Kṛṣṇa himself, together with the people of Vraja, bowed down to that manifestation which was none other than himself, reciting the verse and a half beginning ‘aho.’

37-38.word_for_word: kāma-rūpī — able to assume forms at will; sarpa-ādi-rūpaḥ — such as the form of a serpent; asmai adraye — to this mountain; śarmaṇe — for welfare; kṣemāya — for security; karma eva alam — one proposed view: action alone is sufficient; prāk-svabhāvaḥ guṇaḥ vā — or previous nature / the guṇas; karma-aṅgam vā — or the deity is merely an accessory of karma; tad-vaśaḥ vā maheśaḥ — or the great Lord is subject to karma; vārtā-kartrī devatā iti — or one's occupational support itself is the deity; iyam ṣaṇ-matī — these are the six lines of argument; deva-kṣobhe — used for agitating the god Indra; na tu abhīṣṭā — they are not Kṛṣṇa's finally intended doctrine
37-38.translation: ‘Able to assume forms at will’ includes forms such as that of a serpent; the prayer is ‘may this mountain grant us welfare and security.’ Śrīdhara then summarizes the argumentative positions Kṛṣṇa has deployed: that karma alone is sufficient; that prior nature or the guṇas are the cause; that the deity is merely an accessory to ritual; that even the Supreme Lord is subordinate to karma; that one's actual livelihood is the deity to be served; and related causal formulations. These six argumentative positions are employed to provoke and humble Indra; Śrīdhara explicitly states that they are not Kṛṣṇa's ultimately intended teaching.
